subject: Chemistry
title: Introduction and Matter
outline: Branches of chemistry, careers and the scientific method
Laboratory safety rules and hazard symbols
States of matter and the kinetic theory
Symbols, valency, formulae, balancing and ionic equations

modules.title: 1.1 What Chemistry Is and How Chemists Work
modules.html:
Chemistry is the branch of science that studies the composition, structure, properties and changes of matter. Every material object you can touch — air, water, rock, fuel, food, your own body — is matter, and chemistry explains what it is made of and how it behaves when it meets other matter.

Chemistry is usually divided into five broad branches:

  • Inorganic chemistry — elements and their compounds other than the hydrocarbons (metals, acids, salts, minerals).
  • Organic chemistry — compounds of carbon such as alkanes, alkanols, fats, proteins and plastics.
  • Physical chemistry — the energy, rates and equilibria that govern reactions.
  • Analytical chemistry — finding out what is present (qualitative) and how much is present (quantitative).
  • Biochemistry — the chemistry of living cells.

The scientific method

Chemists do not guess; they follow a disciplined sequence:

  1. Observation — noticing a fact, e.g. "iron nails rust faster near the sea".
  2. Problem statement / question — "does salt speed up rusting?"
  3. Hypothesis — a testable, tentative explanation: "dissolved salt increases the rate of rusting".
  4. Experiment — a fair test with one variable changed at a time and a control kept unchanged.
  5. Data collection and analysis — tables, graphs, averages.
  6. Conclusion — the hypothesis is supported or rejected.
  7. Theory / law — a hypothesis that survives repeated testing becomes a theory; a consistently observed pattern expressed mathematically becomes a law.

Laboratory safety

Safety rules are not decoration — they are chemistry's first lesson:

  • Never eat, drink or taste anything in the laboratory; identify gases by wafting, never by direct sniffing.
  • Always add acid to water, slowly and with stirring, when diluting concentrated acids. The reverse (water to acid) releases heat so violently that the liquid spits.
  • Wear goggles, a laboratory coat and closed shoes; tie back long hair near a Bunsen burner.
  • Heat test tubes with the mouth pointing away from everyone, moving the tube gently in the flame.
  • Know your hazard symbols: corrosive, toxic, flammable, oxidising, irritant/harmful, explosive, radioactive.
  • Work with chlorine, bromine, hydrogen sulphide, sulphur dioxide, nitrogen dioxide and concentrated ammonia inside a fume cupboard.

Chemistry and the Nigerian economy

Chemical industries convert raw materials into useful products: petroleum refining (Port Harcourt, Warri, Kaduna, Dangote Refinery), petrochemicals and plastics, fertilizers (NPK, urea from Indorama and Dangote), cement (limestone → clinker), pharmaceuticals, breweries, soap and detergents, paints, textiles and dyes, and metallurgy (Ajaokuta steel). Careers include chemical engineering, pharmacy, medicine, industrial chemistry, forensic science, food technology, quality control and teaching.

examples.q: State three branches of chemistry and one thing each studies.
examples.a: Inorganic – metals, acids and salts; Organic – carbon compounds such as alkanes and plastics; Physical – energy, rate and equilibrium of reactions.

examples.q: Why must concentrated H2SO4 be added to water and never water to acid?
examples.a: Dilution is strongly exothermic. Adding acid slowly to a large volume of water lets the water absorb and spread the heat; adding water to acid concentrates the heat at the surface and the mixture spits corrosive acid out of the container.

examples.q: Distinguish between a hypothesis and a theory.
examples.a: A hypothesis is a tentative, testable explanation proposed before experimentation; a theory is an explanation that has already survived many independent experimental tests and can predict new results.

modules.title: 1.2 Matter and the Three States
modules.html:
Matter is anything that has mass and occupies space. Every sample of matter is made of extremely small particles — atoms, molecules or ions — that are always in motion. This idea is the kinetic theory of matter, and it explains the three common states.

PropertySolidLiquidGas
ArrangementClose-packed, orderly latticeClose but disorderlyFar apart, random
MotionVibration about fixed pointsSlide over one anotherRapid, random, straight-line
Forces between particlesVery strongModerateNegligible
Shape / volumeFixed shape, fixed volumeNo fixed shape, fixed volumeNeither fixed
CompressibilityAlmost noneVery slightVery high

Changes of state

Melting (solid → liquid), freezing (liquid → solid), vaporisation/boiling (liquid → gas), condensation (gas → liquid), sublimation (solid → gas directly, e.g. iodine, ammonium chloride, solid CO2, camphor) and deposition (gas → solid). All are physical changes: no new substance is formed and the change is easily reversed.

During a change of state the temperature stays constant even though heat is still supplied. That heat, the latent heat, is used to overcome the forces between particles rather than to raise their kinetic energy.

Evidence for the particle theory

  • Diffusion — the smell of perfume spreads across a room; NH3 and HCl gases meet in a tube to form a white ring of NH4Cl nearer the HCl end, because the lighter NH3 diffuses faster.
  • Brownian motion — smoke particles viewed under a microscope jerk about because invisible air molecules bombard them randomly.
  • Osmosis and dissolution — sugar disappears into water because its particles slot into spaces between water molecules; the volume of the mixture is slightly less than the sum of the two volumes.

Physical and chemical change

Physical changeChemical change
No new substanceNew substance(s) formed
Easily reversibleUsually not easily reversible
Little heat changeMarked heat/light change
Mass of substance unchangedMass of each substance changes (total mass conserved)
Melting ice, dissolving salt, magnetising ironRusting, burning, respiration, souring of milk

examples.q: Why does a gas fill its container completely while a liquid does not?
examples.a: Gas particles have negligible forces of attraction and very high kinetic energy, so they move randomly in straight lines until they hit the walls, spreading throughout the container. Liquid particles still attract one another strongly enough to keep a fixed volume.
Iodine and ammonium chloride (also solid carbon dioxide and camphor).

examples.q: Classify: (i) burning of candle wax (ii) melting of candle wax.
examples.a: (i) Chemical change — CO2 and water vapour are new substances and heat and light are given out. (ii) Physical change — only the state changes and the wax can be re-solidified.

modules.title: 1.3 Elements, Compounds and Mixtures
modules.html:
Matter is first classified as a pure substance (fixed composition, sharp melting/boiling point) or a mixture (variable composition, melts/boils over a range). Pure substances are either elements or compounds.

  • Element — a substance that cannot be split into simpler substances by ordinary chemical means, e.g. iron, oxygen, sulphur. There are over 118 known elements, classified as metals, non-metals and metalloids (Si, Ge, As, Sb).
  • Compound — two or more elements chemically combined in a fixed ratio by mass, e.g. water H2O, common salt NaCl, carbon(IV) oxide CO2. Energy is absorbed or evolved when a compound forms and its properties differ completely from those of its elements.
  • Mixture — two or more substances physically together in any proportion, each keeping its own properties, e.g. air, sea water, soil, brass, crude oil.

Compound versus mixture — the iron and sulphur test

Grind iron filings with sulphur powder: the mixture is attracted by a magnet and the sulphur can be dissolved out with carbon disulphide. Heat the same masses strongly and a black solid, iron(II) sulphide FeS, forms; it is not magnetic, does not dissolve in CS2, and gives the rotten-egg gas H2S with dilute HCl. The reaction \(\mathrm{Fe + S \rightarrow FeS}\) requires a fixed 56 : 32 mass ratio.

Types of mixture

A homogeneous mixture has one visible phase throughout (salt solution, air, alloys); a heterogeneous mixture shows separate phases (sand and water, oil and water, granite).

Laws of chemical combination

  • Law of conservation of mass — matter is neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction.
  • Law of constant (definite) proportions — a given pure compound always contains the same elements in the same proportion by mass. Water from any source is 1 part hydrogen to 8 parts oxygen by mass.
  • Law of multiple proportions — when two elements form more than one compound, the masses of one element combining with a fixed mass of the other are in a simple whole-number ratio (CO and CO2: 16 g and 32 g of oxygen per 12 g carbon, ratio 1 : 2).

examples.q: Air is a mixture, not a compound. Give two reasons.
examples.a: Its composition varies from place to place, and its components (N2, O2, CO2, noble gases) keep their individual properties and can be separated by physical means — fractional distillation of liquid air.

examples.q: 8.0 g of copper forms 10.0 g of copper(II) oxide in one experiment and 4.0 g forms 5.0 g in another. Which law does this illustrate?
examples.a: The law of constant proportions: in both cases the Cu : O mass ratio is 8 : 2 = 4 : 1.

modules.title: 1.4 Separation Techniques
modules.html:
Because a mixture is only physically combined, its components can be separated by exploiting a difference in physical properties. Choose the method that matches the difference.

MethodProperty usedTypical use
Handpicking / sievingParticle sizeStones from beans; sand from gravel
Magnetic separationMagnetismIron filings from sulphur
FiltrationSolubility / particle sizeSand from salt solution; chalk from water
Decantation & centrifugingDensityMuddy water; blood cells from plasma
EvaporationVolatility (solvent lost)Recovering salt from brine
CrystallisationSolubility changes with temperaturePurifying copper(II) sulphate, sugar, KNO3
Simple distillationBoiling point (solvent recovered)Pure water from sea water
Fractional distillationDifferent boiling points of miscible liquidsEthanol/water; crude oil; liquid air
Separating funnelImmiscibility and densityKerosene and water; oil and water
SublimationOne solid sublimesAmmonium chloride from sodium chloride; iodine from sand
ChromatographyDifferent rates of movement on a mediumDyes in ink, plant pigments, drug testing
PrecipitationFormation of insoluble solidRemoving Ca2+ from hard water

Fractional distillation in detail

A fractionating column packed with glass beads or fitted with plates provides a large surface for repeated vaporisation and condensation. The vapour richest in the more volatile liquid rises highest; the less volatile liquid condenses and drips back. Ethanol (b.p. 78 °C) distils before water (100 °C). In crude-oil refining, the column is hottest at the base: bitumen > lubricating oil > diesel > kerosene > petrol > refinery gas as you rise.

Paper chromatography

A spot of mixture is placed on the base line of chromatography paper (the stationary phase) above the level of a solvent (the mobile phase). As solvent rises, components travel different distances according to their solubility in the solvent and their adsorption on the paper. The retardation factor is

\( R_f = \dfrac{\text{distance moved by solute}}{\text{distance moved by solvent front}} \)

\(R_f\) is always less than 1 and is characteristic of a substance in a given solvent, so it can be used to identify components.

examples.q: How would you obtain pure water from ink?
examples.a: Simple distillation: heat the ink, condense the steam in a Liebig condenser and collect the distillate — pure water; the dye remains in the flask.

examples.q: A solute moves 4.5 cm while the solvent front moves 9.0 cm. Find Rf.
Which method separates a mixture of sodium chloride and ammonium chloride?
examples.a: Sublimation — on heating, ammonium chloride sublimes and re-solidifies on a cool surface, leaving sodium chloride behind.

modules.title: 1.5 Symbols, Formulae and Chemical Equations
modules.html:
Each element has an international symbol — one capital letter, or a capital plus a small letter: H, O, C, N, Na (natrium), K (kalium), Fe (ferrum), Cu (cuprum), Ag (argentum), Au (aurum), Pb (plumbum), Sn (stannum), Hg (hydrargyrum), Sb (stibium).

Valency and formula writing

Valency is the combining power of an atom or radical. Write the symbols side by side, then exchange (criss-cross) the valencies as subscripts and simplify.

Valency 1Valency 2Valency 3
Na+, K+, H+, NH4+, Cl−, NO3−, OH−, HCO3−Mg2+, Ca2+, Zn2+, Fe2+, Cu2+, O2−, SO42−, CO32−Al3+, Fe3+, PO43−

Example: aluminium sulphate — Al3+ and SO42− → Al2(SO4)3. Calcium carbonate — Ca2+ and CO32− → CaCO3 (subscripts cancel).

Balancing equations

A chemical equation must obey the law of conservation of mass: the number of atoms of each element must be the same on both sides. Never change a formula to balance — change only the coefficients.

  • \( \mathrm{2H_2 + O_2 \rightarrow 2H_2O} \)
  • \( \mathrm{CH_4 + 2O_2 \rightarrow CO_2 + 2H_2O} \)
  • \( \mathrm{Fe_2O_3 + 3CO \rightarrow 2Fe + 3CO_2} \)
  • \( \mathrm{2KClO_3 \xrightarrow{\ \Delta\ } 2KCl + 3O_2} \)
  • \( \mathrm{Zn + H_2SO_4 \rightarrow ZnSO_4 + H_2} \)

State symbols are added in brackets: (s) solid, (l) liquid, (g) gas, (aq) aqueous solution, e.g. \( \mathrm{AgNO_3(aq) + NaCl(aq) \rightarrow AgCl(s) + NaNO_3(aq)} \).

Ionic equations

Spectator ions — those unchanged on both sides — are cancelled. The reaction above becomes simply \( \mathrm{Ag^+(aq) + Cl^-(aq) \rightarrow AgCl(s)} \). Neutralisation of any strong acid by any strong alkali reduces to \( \mathrm{H^+(aq) + OH^-(aq) \rightarrow H_2O(l)} \).

examples.q: Write the formula of iron(III) sulphate.
Write the ionic equation for the reaction of dilute HCl with sodium hydroxide.
examples.a: H+(aq) + OH−(aq) → H2O(l); Na+ and Cl− are spectator ions.

quiz.q: Chemistry is best defined as the study of
options: the motion of bodies under forces
the composition, properties and changes of matter
the structure of the earth's crust
quiz.solution: Chemistry deals with matter: what it is made of, how it behaves and how it changes.

quiz.q: Which branch of chemistry deals mainly with carbon compounds?
quiz.solution: Organic chemistry is the chemistry of carbon compounds such as hydrocarbons, alkanols and polymers.

quiz.q: A tentative, testable explanation proposed before experimenting is a
quiz.solution: A hypothesis is the tentative explanation that the experiment is designed to test.

quiz.q: In a fair experiment, the set-up kept unchanged for comparison is the
quiz.solution: The control provides a baseline against which the changed set-up is compared.

quiz.q: When diluting concentrated sulphuric acid you should
options: add water to the acid quickly
add acid to water slowly with stirring
mix equal volumes in a stoppered bottle
heat the acid before adding water
quiz.solution: Dilution is highly exothermic; adding acid to a large volume of water disperses the heat and prevents spitting.

quiz.q: Gases such as chlorine should be prepared in a
quiz.solution: A fume cupboard removes toxic vapours safely.

quiz.q: The correct way to detect the smell of a gas in the laboratory is to
options: inhale deeply over the mouth of the tube
waft a little of the gas towards the nose
taste a drop of the condensate
quiz.solution: Wafting brings only a trace of gas to the nose and avoids poisoning.

quiz.q: Matter is anything that
options: can be seen with the eye
quiz.solution: That is the standard definition of matter.

quiz.q: The particles of a solid
quiz.solution: In a solid, strong forces hold particles in a lattice where they only vibrate.

quiz.q: Which state of matter has a fixed volume but no fixed shape?
quiz.solution: A liquid keeps its volume but takes the shape of its container.

quiz.q: The random movement of smoke particles seen under a microscope is called
quiz.solution: Brownian motion results from bombardment by invisible air molecules.

quiz.q: Which of these substances sublimes on heating?
quiz.solution: Ammonium chloride passes directly from solid to vapour and re-forms as a solid on a cool surface.

quiz.q: During melting, the temperature of a pure solid
quiz.solution: The heat supplied (latent heat of fusion) breaks the forces between particles instead of raising temperature.

quiz.q: Which is a chemical change?
quiz.solution: Rusting forms hydrated iron(III) oxide, a new substance, and is not easily reversed.

quiz.q: A substance that cannot be split into simpler substances by chemical means is a(n)
quiz.solution: That is the definition of an element.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a compound?
quiz.solution: Sodium chloride has elements chemically combined in a fixed ratio; the others are mixtures.

quiz.q: A mixture of iron filings and sulphur can be separated with a magnet because
options: each keeps its own properties in a mixture
quiz.solution: Components of a mixture retain their individual physical properties.

quiz.q: When iron and sulphur are heated together the product FeS is
options: a new compound with different properties
quiz.solution: A chemical reaction has occurred, giving a compound with entirely new properties.

quiz.q: Air is regarded as a mixture because
options: its composition varies and components keep their properties
quiz.solution: Variable composition and retained properties are the hallmarks of a mixture.

quiz.q: Water from a river and water from a well both contain hydrogen and oxygen in the mass ratio 1 : 8. This illustrates the law of
quiz.solution: A pure compound always has the same composition by mass.

quiz.q: Carbon forms CO and CO2. The masses of oxygen combining with 12 g of carbon are 16 g and 32 g, a ratio of 1 : 2. This illustrates the law of
quiz.solution: Simple whole-number ratios of one element with a fixed mass of another define the law of multiple proportions.

quiz.q: Which technique separates sand from a salt solution?
quiz.solution: Sand is insoluble and is retained as residue on the filter paper.

quiz.q: Pure water is best obtained from sea water by
quiz.solution: Distillation vaporises the water and condenses it, leaving dissolved solids behind.

quiz.q: Two miscible liquids with different boiling points are best separated by
quiz.solution: A fractionating column allows repeated vaporisation and condensation, separating by boiling point.

quiz.q: Kerosene and water are separated using a
quiz.solution: They are immiscible and of different densities, so they form two layers that can be run off separately.

quiz.q: In paper chromatography the paper is the
quiz.solution: The paper holds the components; the solvent that moves is the mobile phase.

quiz.q: A component travels 3 cm while the solvent front travels 12 cm. Its Rf value is
The Rf value of a substance is always
quiz.solution: The solute cannot travel farther than the solvent front, so Rf < 1.

quiz.q: Which method is used to purify copper(II) sulphate crystals?
quiz.solution: A saturated hot solution is cooled so that pure crystals separate, leaving impurities in the mother liquor.

quiz.q: In the fractional distillation of crude oil the fraction collected at the highest point of the column is
quiz.solution: The most volatile fraction rises highest before condensing.

quiz.q: The symbol for potassium is
quiz.solution: K comes from the Latin kalium; P is phosphorus.

quiz.q: The symbol Pb represents
quiz.solution: Pb is from the Latin plumbum, meaning lead.

quiz.q: The valency of the sulphate radical is
quiz.solution: SO4^2− carries two negative charges.

quiz.q: The formula of aluminium sulphate is
quiz.solution: Criss-crossing Al3+ and SO4^2− gives Al2(SO4)3.

quiz.q: The formula of ammonium carbonate is
quiz.solution: NH4+ has valency 1 and CO3^2− has valency 2, so two ammonium ions are needed.

quiz.q: Balancing: Al + O2 → Al2O3. The coefficients are
quiz.solution: 4Al + 3O2 → 2Al2O3 balances 4 Al and 6 O on each side.

quiz.q: In the equation 2KClO3 → 2KCl + 3O2, the number of moles of oxygen gas from 2 moles of KClO3 is
quiz.solution: The coefficient of O2 is 3.

quiz.q: The state symbol (aq) means the substance is
quiz.solution: (aq) stands for aqueous, i.e. dissolved in water.

quiz.q: Ions that appear unchanged on both sides of an ionic equation are called
quiz.solution: Spectator ions are cancelled out when writing the net ionic equation.

quiz.q: The ionic equation for the neutralisation of a strong acid by a strong alkali is
quiz.solution: Only the hydrogen and hydroxide ions actually react.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a physical change?
quiz.solution: Burning magnesium forms magnesium oxide, a new substance.

quiz.q: A homogeneous mixture is one that
quiz.solution: Homogeneous mixtures such as salt solution or brass look the same throughout.

quiz.q: Which apparatus is used to condense vapour during distillation?
quiz.solution: The Liebig condenser carries cold water in its outer jacket to condense the vapour.

quiz.q: A metalloid among the following is
quiz.solution: Silicon shows both metallic and non-metallic properties.

quiz.q: A pure substance is characterised by
quiz.solution: Impurities lower and broaden the melting point; a pure solid melts sharply.

quiz.q: Which industry converts limestone into clinker?
quiz.solution: Cement manufacture roasts limestone with clay to form clinker.

quiz.q: The hazard symbol showing a skull and crossbones means the substance is
quiz.solution: The skull and crossbones warns of a toxic (poisonous) substance.

quiz.q: Centrifuging separates a mixture on the basis of difference in
quiz.solution: Rapid spinning forces the denser particles to the bottom of the tube.

quiz.q: Ammonia gas diffuses faster than hydrogen chloride gas because it
quiz.solution: Lighter molecules diffuse faster, so the white NH4Cl ring forms nearer the HCl end.

quiz.q: The law of conservation of mass states that in a chemical reaction, mass is
quiz.solution: Total mass of reactants equals total mass of products.
